structure.title: Books I–IV · A refugee at another founder's table
structure.text: A storm delivers Aeneas to Carthage. At Dido's invitation he tells of Troy's destruction and the exiles' wandering. His listener has fled violence herself and already achieved the difficult thing he hopes to do, found a city.

structure.title: Books V–VI · The living consult the dead
structure.text: Funeral games honour Aeneas's father. Later the son seeks him in the underworld, where family affection meets a vision of the people Rome will one day call its own. Knowledge of a glorious future can also impose a heavy obligation.

structure.title: Books VII–XII · Someone already lives in Italy
structure.text: A marriage proposal, a hunting accident and appeals to allies draw households into war. The destination long promised to the Trojans is a country whose inhabitants have understandable ideas about their children's future.

people.name: Aeneas
people.text: He carries memories and sacred objects out of a ruined city. What he owes the dead frequently cuts across what he wants as a living man. His responsibilities extend to people he will never see.

people.name: Dido
people.text: When Aeneas meets her she is watching walls rise and allotting work. Her capacity as a ruler makes the personal and public consequences of taking in the Trojans unusually hard to separate.

people.name: Turnus and Lavinia
people.role: A local claimant and the king's daughter
people.text: Their expected marriage has implications for Italian power. A new claimant from overseas turns a family decision into a dispute about whose descendants will rule. Lavinia herself gets little say in the negotiations.

context.title: Rome lies in the future
context.text: Aeneas will never walk the streets of imperial Rome. Its history enters his story through prophecies, images and the narrator's knowledge. A person staring at a picture may understand less of its significance than a Roman reader.

notice.text: What does a person carry out of danger?
notice.why: A father, a child, household gods and captured equipment all have histories. Objects kept as proofs of survival or victory may later be recognised by someone with entirely different memories.

notice.text: Listen for the names of parents when a young fighter appears.
notice.why: The narrator can see past a warrior's moment of glory to the household awaiting his return. The promised survival of a people gives individual parents little protection.

opening: Aeneas escapes the destruction of Troy carrying his father and leading his young son. Survival should be enough, but the gods require him to carry a future civilisation as well. He must find a home for his people, even when the places and people he encounters offer reasons to stop travelling. Virgil gives Rome a magnificent origin and lets the losses remain visible inside it: love interrupted, lives spent, and a promised greatness whose beneficiaries have not yet been born.
